title: Paul and His Influence on Christianity
subtitle: How to assess a claimed revelation without erasing Paul's real apostolic connections
summary: Paul's influence is undeniable, but influence alone neither validates his claimed revelation nor proves that he invented Christianity. His letters preserve received traditions and contacts with Jesus's earlier followers as well as disputes. Islam's disagreement concerns the authority of his Christ-centered gospel, which must be evaluated alongside the independent evidence for the Quran and Muhammad.

seo.metaTitle: Paul and His Influence on Christianity - Islamic and Christian Perspectives
seo.metaDescription: Paul's claimed revelation, received tradition, apostolic contacts, and influence—and the actual question Islam raises about his authority.

sections.title: The Question Is Authority, Not a Villain
sections.body:
Islam does not need Paul to be dishonest or the sole inventor of Christianity. Its disagreement is whether the gospel centered on Christ's saving death faithfully carries God's guidance. Paul is important because he makes that claim clearly, not because every later doctrine can be blamed on him.

The same standard must apply to Islam: [Who Is Prophet Muhammad?](/articles/who-is-prophet-muhammad) examines another prophetic claim, and [Why the Quran?](/articles/why-the-quran) asks what supports its authority. Disagreeing with Paul cannot itself establish either.

sections.title: What His Own Testimony Says
sections.body:
Galatians 1:11–17 presents Paul's gospel as received through revelation of Jesus Christ and describes his earlier persecution of the movement. Acts 9:1–16 narrates his encounter and calling from another author's perspective.

No secure source establishes that Paul accompanied Jesus during his public ministry. That is different from proving he never saw Jesus at any earlier moment. His own claim is to a later revelation, whose truth requires assessment rather than an assumption that either sincerity or lateness settles the matter.

sections.title: A Claimed Vision Needs Grounds for Trust
sections.body:
A profound experience can explain a person's conviction and change of life without establishing every conclusion drawn from it. Paul claims more than personal inspiration: he claims divine authority for the message he proclaims.

The appropriate questions concern testimony, the content of the message, its relationship to earlier guidance, and the credibility of the wider claim. Calling the experience private is not a complete refutation. Many religious claims begin with an experience others did not share, including claims within Islam.

sections.title: Paul Did Not Present Himself as Inventing the Gospel
sections.body:
In 1 Corinthians 15:1–11, Paul makes death for sins, burial, resurrection, and appearances central. Crucially, he says he received and transmitted the message and connects it with other apostles.

That is evidence against an easy theory that Paul alone created belief in Christ's saving death and resurrection. The passage's claim of continuity still needs evaluation, but the claim is there. A disagreement with his theology should not require deleting what his own source says.

sections.title: Faith, Law, and Moral Conduct
sections.body:
Romans 3:28 places justification—right standing before God—through faith apart from works of the law. Ephesians 2:8–9 also emphasizes grace; its traditional Pauline attribution and scholarly disputes about authorship are distinct questions from what the text teaches.

Paul's position cannot be reduced to permission for immoral conduct. The question of non-Jewish believers and circumcision is also not identical to abolishing every Jewish practice for every believer. His [discussion of circumcision](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/galatians/5) and [advice about existing status](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/1corinthians/7) make that distinction relevant.

sections.title: Connections With the Earlier Apostles
sections.body:
In the [later part of Galatians' first chapter](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/galatians/1), Paul reports meeting Cephas, or Peter, and James. In [the next chapter](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/galatians/2), he describes recognition of his mission by James, Cephas, and John, alongside his confrontation with Cephas over table fellowship.

These reports show connection and conflict, not total isolation. They are Paul's account of those relationships, not a complete transcript accepted without question. They nevertheless prevent a claim that he was simply unknown to the people who had followed Jesus.

sections.title: An Objection: Does Apostolic Recognition Settle It?
sections.body:
A Christian can argue that received tradition and contact with Jerusalem leaders strongly support Paul's continuity with the earliest movement. That is substantive evidence and gives a better account than a lone-inventor theory.

It does not, by itself, establish that the message is divine or that every theological inference is correct. Recognition within a community supports a claim to represent that community; its authority from God still depends on the wider case. The Muslim disagreement must address that case rather than treat every internal dispute as proof of complete rupture.

sections.title: The Difference Between Influence and Truth
sections.body:
Paul's letters became authoritative Christian texts and have shaped Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant theology. Those traditions interpret his account of faith, grace, and works differently, as discussed in [Grace, Mercy, Faith, and Deeds](/articles/grace-mercy-faith-deeds).

Widespread influence explains why Paul matters. It does not prove truth, any more than controversial influence proves falsehood. The proper focus is his actual teaching and the evidence offered for its authority, not an imagined hidden motive.

sections.title: Where Islam's Judgment Differs
sections.body:
Quran 3:79 denies that a prophet would call people to serve him instead of God. Quran 5:77 warns against excess in religion, and 4:157 conflicts with the crucifixion on which Paul's account of salvation depends.

The Quran does not name Paul. Identifying every criticism of Christians with an accusation against him would go beyond the text. The Islamic judgment is instead about the content and authority of the message: Jesus is honored as God's messenger, not treated as a divine savior whose death is the foundation of pardon.

sections.title: What the Question Changes in Practice
sections.body:
The dispute leads to worship and repentance, not merely a verdict on an ancient personality. [What Is Worship?](/articles/what-is-worship) examines why Islam directs devotion to the Creator alone; [Forgiveness in Islam and Christianity](/articles/forgiveness-in-islam-and-christianity) examines the role attributed to Christ's death.

Neither Muslim criticism nor Christian admiration should substitute for reading the sources. Paul can be taken seriously as a historical witness while his claim to guide belief remains open to scrutiny.

sections.title: A Specific Next Step
sections.body:
The most useful comparison is between Paul's own received-tradition claim in 1 Corinthians 15:1–11 and the evidence for the Quran's different account of Jesus. [The Historical Jesus](/articles/the-historical-jesus) keeps the historical difficulty visible rather than assuming it away.

Islam's invitation is to judge a message by its grounds, worship the one God, and return to Him sincerely—not to make rejection of Paul a substitute for a reasoned faith.

quranVerses.arabic: قُلْ يَٰٓأَهْلَ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ لَا تَغْلُوا۟ فِى دِينِكُمْ غَيْرَ ٱلْحَقِّ وَلَا تَتَّبِعُوٓا۟ أَهْوَآءَ قَوْمٍۢ قَدْ ضَلُّوا۟ مِن قَبْلُ وَأَضَلُّوا۟ كَثِيرًۭا وَضَلُّوا۟ عَن سَوَآءِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ
quranVerses.translation: Say, "O People of the Scripture, do not exceed limits in your religion beyond the truth and do not follow the inclinations of a people who had gone astray before and misled many and have strayed from the soundness of the way."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: مَا كَانَ لِبَشَرٍ أَن يُؤْتِيَهُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَٱلْحُكْمَ وَٱلنُّبُوَّةَ ثُمَّ يَقُولَ لِلنَّاسِ كُونُوا۟ عِبَادًۭا لِّى مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ وَلَٰكِن كُونُوا۟ رَبَّٰنِيِّۦنَ بِمَا كُنتُمْ تُعَلِّمُونَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ وَبِمَا كُنتُمْ تَدْرُسُونَ
quranVerses.translation: It is not for a human [prophet] that Allah should give him the Scripture and authority and prophethood and then he would say to the people, "Be servants to me rather than Allah," but [instead, he would say], "Be pious scholars of the Lord because of what you have taught of the Scripture and because of what you have studied."
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَمِنَ ٱلَّذِينَ قَالُوٓا۟ إِنَّا نَصَٰرَىٰٓ أَخَذْنَا مِيثَٰقَهُمْ فَنَسُوا۟ حَظًّۭا مِّمَّا ذُكِّرُوا۟ بِهِۦ فَأَغْرَيْنَا بَيْنَهُمُ ٱلْعَدَاوَةَ وَٱلْبَغْضَآءَ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ ۚ وَسَوْفَ يُنَبِّئُهُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِمَا كَانُوا۟ يَصْنَعُونَ
quranVerses.translation: And from those who say, "We are Christians" We took their covenant; but they forgot a portion of that of which they were reminded. So We caused among them animosity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection. And Allah is going to inform them about what they used to do.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا
quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: But I make known to you, brothers, concerning the Good News which was preached by me, that it is not according to man. For neither did I receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ. For you have heard of my way of living in time past in the Jews’ religion, how that beyond measure I persecuted the assembly of God, and ravaged it. I advanced in the Jews’ religion beyond many of my own age among my countrymen, being more exceedingly zealous for the traditions of my fathers. But when it was the good pleasure of God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles, I didn’t immediately confer with flesh and blood, nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia. Then I returned to Damascus.

Now I declare to you, brothers, the Good News which I preached to you, which also you received, in which you also stand, by which also you are saved, if you hold firmly the word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain. For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also. For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Whether then it is I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.
We maintain therefore that a man is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.
for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.

But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest, and asked for letters from him to the synagogues of Damascus, that if he found any who were of the Way, whether men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. As he traveled, he got close to Damascus, and suddenly a light from the sky shone around him. He fell on the earth, and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He said, “Who are you, Lord?” The Lord said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise up, and enter into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” The men who traveled with him stood speechless, hearing the sound, but seeing no one. Saul arose from the ground, and when his eyes were opened, he saw no one. They led him by the hand, and brought him into Damascus. He was without sight for three days, and neither ate nor drank. Now there was a certain disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias!” He said, “Behold, it’s me, Lord.” The Lord said to him, “Arise, and go to the street which is called Straight, and inquire in the house of Judah for one named Saul, a man of Tarsus. For behold, he is praying, and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias coming in, and laying his hands on him, that he might receive his sight.” But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he did to your saints at Jerusalem. Here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” But the Lord said to him, “Go your way, for he is my chosen vessel to bear my name before the nations and kings, and the children of Israel. For I will show him how many things he must suffer for my name’s sake.”

faq.question: Was Paul entirely unknown to the earlier apostles?
faq.answer: No. Galatians reports meetings, recognition of his mission, and conflict with Jerusalem leaders. Those are significant connections even though the reports come from Paul's own account.

faq.question: Did Paul claim to invent belief in Jesus's death and resurrection?
faq.answer: No. In 1 Corinthians 15:1–11 he describes a received tradition and connects his proclamation with other apostles.

faq.question: Does the Quran name Paul as the source of Christian error?
faq.answer: No. Its criticism of theological claims must not be turned into a named accusation that the text does not make.

faq.question: Does not accompanying Jesus automatically disprove Paul's revelation claim?
faq.answer: No. It identifies the kind of claim that needs assessment. A later claimed revelation requires grounds for trust; lateness alone does not decide it.

faq.question: Does disagreeing with Paul prove Muhammad's claim?
faq.answer: No. Islam needs a positive case for its own revelation and messenger, evaluated by a consistent standard.

furtherReading.title: Paul: The Apostle's Life, Letters, and Thought
furtherReading.author: E.P. Sanders
furtherReading.note: A comprehensive scholarly examination of Paul's biography, epistles, and theological framework, drawing on both historical-critical and textual analysis to assess Paul's historical development and religious thought.

furtherReading.title: Paul and the Faithfulness of God
furtherReading.author: N.T. Wright
furtherReading.note: A major study integrating Paul's theology within Jewish covenantal thought and early Christian ecclesiology, examining how Paul understood the continuity between Jewish scripture and Christian faith in Jesus.

furtherReading.title: Paul Among Jews and Gentiles
furtherReading.author: Krister Stendahl
furtherReading.note: A classical work reassessing Paul's position on Jewish law and his relationship with other apostles, with particular attention to the theological question of how Gentiles were incorporated into God's people without full proselyte conversion.

furtherReading.title: Paul: A Critical Life
furtherReading.author: Jerome Murphy-O'Connor
furtherReading.note: A detailed biographical and critical study of Paul's missionary journeys, his theological development, and the social context of the early Christian communities he founded and addressed in his letters.
